title: Hebous & Mengistu, "Efficient Economic Rent Taxation under a Global Minimum Corporate Tax" (Oxford CBT WP 24/10, 6 Aug 2024; also IMF WP 2024/057; SSRN 4868726)

Also a candidate light ENRICH for concepts/allowance-for-corporate-equity.md and research/hebous-ruf-ace.md See Also, since the paper's central result concerns ACE specifically (ACE is worse-affected by the minimum tax than cash-flow taxation).
claim_grade: A-claim, Tier 1. Working paper by IMF Fiscal Affairs Department staff (Hebous, Mengistu) circulated jointly as an Oxford CBT working paper -- an official/standing body under EDITORIAL SS4c (IMF), and Hebous is already an established Tier-1 name on this wiki (three prior cited papers: hebous-excess-profit-taxes.md, hebous-ruf-ace.md, and cash-flow-tax.md's source 12). Strong evidence the paper has since cleared peer review: a same-author, near-identical-abstract article appears in IMF Economic Review (a Springer-published, peer-reviewed journal; the wiki already cites this exact journal for a different Hebous paper on cash-flow-tax.md). This inference rests on matching authors + overlapping abstract + a natural WP-to-journal title change, not on a side-by-side text comparison of the two versions (not obtained).
content_summary: Core result: the OECD/G20 'Pillar Two' 15% global minimum corporate tax breaks the previously-established equivalence between the two efficient rent-tax designs, the R-based cash-flow tax and the allowance for corporate equity (ACE) -- both are neutral (zero marginal effective tax rate, METR) on a stand-alone basis, but the minimum tax's top-up mechanism treats them asymmetrically. Mechanism: Pillar Two's top-up tax applies when the ratio of covered tax to covered profit (GloBE income) falls below 15%, on a base of profit minus the substance-based income exclusion (SBIE, = 5% of tangible assets plus payroll, after a transition period). Immediate expensing (the cash-flow tax's mechanism) is treated by the GloBE rules as a 'temporary timing measure' that leaves the Pillar Two effective rate unchanged, so cash-flow taxation per se does not trigger the top-up tax. The ACE's notional deduction, by contrast, is added back into the top-up base and (if refundable) into covered income, which both lowers the Pillar Two effective rate and raises the top-up base -- so 'whenever the top-up binds under the R-based cash-flow tax, it must bind under ACE; but it may bind under ACE while not being binding for the R-based cash-flow tax.' Three regions result: (i) minimum tax binds under both, with a higher top-up tax and METR under ACE; (ii) minimum tax binds only under ACE (cash-flow tax stays at zero METR); (iii) statutory rate high enough (well above 15%) that neither binds and the original equivalence is restored. Policy conclusion: a country combining an R-based cash-flow tax with a statutory CIT rate of at least 15% keeps a zero METR on all investment (in-scope and out-of-scope of Pillar Two alike), 'rendering a two-tier system redundant' -- a straightforwardly superior design on efficiency grounds versus a standard CIT below 15% or an ACE. The paper also separately shows (without any minimum tax) that dropping the 'full loss offset' assumption alone breaks the cash-flow/ACE equivalence, with ACE giving a lower METR than cash-flow taxation in that case. It flags a recurring literature error: several official/institutional studies (CBO 2017, US Treasury 2021, OECD 2023, an EU Commission study) report negative METRs for ACE systems, which is theoretically impossible for a correctly specified rent tax; the paper attributes this to a modeling error (amplifying the allowance beyond the true book value of first-period equity) that 'can easily underestimate the METR by multiple percentage points' (no single point estimate given in the sections read). Its own recommended fix for minimum-tax design: define the top-up base as 'EBIT minus investment' (a cash-flow-like base with carryforward), which would make the minimum tax compatible with any efficient rent-tax design. The companion published version (IMF Economic Review, 2026) adds a cross-country application showing jurisdictions with statutory rates below 15% see higher effective tax rates once the top-up tax applies than in the pre-Pillar-Two baseline (no specific percentage-point magnitude captured from the abstract alone).
existing_wiki_coverage: concepts/cash-flow-tax.md already documents the cash-flow tax / ACE equivalence (citing Boadway & Bruce 1984) and DBCFT variants, with an 'Honest Limits' section on revenue volatility (citing a different Hebous paper, Hebous/Klemm/Stausholm 2020) -- but nothing yet on how the global minimum tax interacts with either design; this paper is a direct, previously-missing fill for that gap. research/hebous-excess-profit-taxes.md (IMF WP/22/187, Hebous/Prihardini/Vernon) already treats ACE/ACC-style rent taxation as the efficient design for excess-profit/windfall taxes but predates Pillar Two implementation discussion. research/hebous-ruf-ace.md (Hebous & Ruf 2017, JPubE) is the wiki's key empirical ACE evaluation (German multinational data) and is a natural cross-link since this new paper is a theoretical extension of exactly the ACE-vs-cash-flow question that paper's 'double dip' finding also concerns. No existing wiki page currently mentions Pillar Two, GloBE, or the substance-based income exclusion by name (checked against the supplied corpus digest, ~1,000 entries) -- this would be the wiki's first coverage of the global minimum tax's interaction with rent-tax design.
uncertainties: (1) The formal derivation sections, numerical-simulation tables, and figures (roughly pages 10-30 of the 63-page PDF) were not read in the depth the wiki's existing hebous-excess-profit-taxes.md page states for its own source ('read in full, 37 pages') -- a T1 writer should read those sections before drafting exact numeric claims (e.g., the specific statutory-rate boundaries of the three regions beyond the headline 15% figure, and the exact percentage-point size of the ACE METR-underestimation error, which the text characterizes only as 'multiple percentage points'). (2) The identification of the IMF Economic Review article as the peer-reviewed version of this same working paper rests on matching authors, near-identical/overlapping abstract content, and a retitling consistent with this wiki's already-documented Hebous WP-to-IMF-Economic-Review publication pattern -- not on a direct read of the published article body, which is paywalled beyond its abstract (Springer's landing page returned a bot-check challenge to a direct fetch; the abstract was obtained via r.jina.ai). A T1 with journal access should confirm before stating on-wiki that the working paper 'has been published' rather than 'a closely related paper by the same authors has been published.' (3) The specific numeric magnitude of the published version's cross-country ETR-gap finding (jurisdictions below 15% facing higher ETRs post-Pillar-Two) is stated only qualitatively in its abstract; no percentage-point figure was captured.

title: Horace Bartilow, "Financialization and the global decline of liberal democracy: The mediating effects of rentier capitalism," The Social Science Journal, published online 12 Sep 2026
what_was_fetched: A direct curl with a browser user-agent to the DOI resolver returned Taylor & Francis's Cloudflare bot-check page (HTTP 403, 'Just a moment...'). Retrieved via r.jina.ai (https://r.jina.ai/https://doi.org/10.1080/03623319.2026.2727907, HTTP 200): this returned the full public landing page as rendered for a non-subscriber -- the complete abstract, author/affiliation line, acknowledgments, footnotes 1-5, and the article's own reference list for those footnotes, but NOT the article body (Introduction, literature review, data/measures, results, discussion), which is paywalled (a 'PDF download + Online access' purchase option for USD 56 is shown on the same page). Also fetched the synapsesocial.com mirror named in the queue context (both a direct curl of the raw Next.js HTML and an r.jina.ai render of it): it offers only a short third-party 'Overview' and bullet-point 'Key Points' summary that appears to restate the abstract without adding new detail, no downloadable full text. Cross-checked bibliographic metadata via Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1080/03623319.2026.2727907): journal The Social Science Journal, pages 1-22, 122 references, publisher Informa UK Limited (Taylor & Francis), author affiliation 'School of International Service, Washington DC, USA.' A WebSearch pass for an open preprint/working-paper copy (SSRN, RePEc, author-hosted PDF) found none. Fetched Horace Bartilow's American University CV directly (https://www.american.edu/uploads/docs/cv11.pdf, HTTP 200) to verify his academic standing: full Professor, International Political Economy & American Foreign Policy, American University School of International Service (2021-present), previously Professor of Political Science, University of Kentucky (1995-2021; Assistant 1995, Associate 2001, full 2010), Ph.D. International Political Economy, SUNY Albany (1994), author of the university-press book Drug War Pathologies: Embedded Corporatism and U.S. Drug Enforcement in the Americas -- this CV copy does not yet list the 2026 Social Science Journal article, consistent with it being very recent.
verdict: Primary recommendation: ENRICH concepts/rentier.md (add a subsection to 'Modern Rentier-Capitalism Literature' on the same abstract-only pattern the page already uses for Kapoor 2026, Smith & Wood 2026, and Palma 2026 -- each explicitly flagged there as 'only the abstract is publicly available ... unverified here') and ENRICH research/christophers-rentier-capitalism.md's See Also (the paper's title names 'rentier capitalism' directly, and Christophers's page is the wiki's anchor research entry for that term). A dedicated NEW research/ page is defensible by the same abstract-only precedent already established on rentier.md, but is a weaker case here than for those three: (a) the paper's own 'rentier class' operationalization (see content_summary) is an aggregate top-1%/top-10% income-share proxy, not a land- or property-rent measurement, so it does not strengthen the wiki's land-specific evidence base the way a Christophers- or Ryan-Collins-style source would; (b) there is no existing problems/ or benefits/ or objections/ page on democracy or democratic backsliding for a new research page's `supports_outcomes`/`bears_on_objections` fields to wire into, so a NEW page would currently be an island reachable only via See Also links; (c) Scan Depth would be Light (abstract only) on a 22-page, 122-reference peer-reviewed article -- below the Medium-minimum target EDITORIAL sets for Important-tier sources. If a T1 judges the empirical contribution (191-country causal-mediation panel result) substantial enough to warrant a page despite these two limits, DEFER is the honest alternative verdict: hold for full-text access (institutional journal access or purchase) before drafting, and open a DEEPEN-SCAN backlog item in the meantime.
claim_grade: A-claim for the abstract sentences themselves (peer-reviewed, Crossref-indexed journal article); Tier 1 by the SS4c rubric for the author -- Bartilow is a tenured full professor with an established, decades-long peer-reviewed and university-press publication record in international political economy (confirmed independently via his American University CV and corroborating web search results), satisfying 'established academics with a peer-reviewed body of work,' even though that prior body of work is in a different IPE subfield (drug-enforcement political economy) rather than rentier-capitalism/financialization specifically -- this journal article appears to be part of a newer research direction (a 2023 profile found via web search describes him as working on a book with this same title). Every claim beyond the abstract's own wording -- the specific financialization index, the specific democracy measure (very likely, but not confirmed, V-Dem's Liberal Democracy Index given the paper's title and field convention), control variables, coefficient sizes, and the mediation proportion -- is a D-claim: unverified, full text not accessible through any access-ladder rung attempted.
content_summary: From the verified abstract: cross-national panel of 191 countries, 2000-2017. Framed explicitly as testing a 'neo-Marxist' capitalism-democracy-contradiction thesis against a stated puzzle: the orthodox democracy-development literature explains liberal democracy's post-1900 global expansion but not its 'precipitous decline over the past 15 years.' Method: mediation structural equation modeling. Finding: financialization significantly increases 'the rentier class's share of national income (the top 1 and 10 percentiles)', and financialization's negative effect on liberal democracy is 'fully mediated' through this rentier-income channel (i.e., no significant direct effect once the income-share channel is accounted for, per the abstract's own framing). Robustness: a sensitivity analysis using an 'Ant Colony Optimization Algorithm' (an unusual, worth-noting robustness technique) shows the mediated result is insensitive to an unobserved confounding 'phantom' variable. Two keywords captured: 'Democratic backsliding,' 'capitalism' (the scrape may have truncated a longer list). Key judgment call the task asked me to make: the paper's 'rentier class' is operationalized purely as top-1%/top-10% national-income-share percentiles -- a Piketty-style top-income-share proxy in the neo-Marxist class-power tradition -- not as a sectoral or asset-based decomposition (land, finance, IP, platforms) the way Christophers's book frames 'rentier capitalism,' and not as any direct land- or property-rent measure. On the evidence available (abstract only), this paper does NOT measure land or property rent specifically. One incidental oddity worth flagging to a T1 who obtains the full text: the acknowledgments state an earlier version of the manuscript was presented at a conference 'on March 8-11, 2003' -- apparently inconsistent with a paper analyzing data through 2017 and accepted in August 2026; likely a publisher/production typo in the acknowledgments text, not something to resolve or repeat without the actual article.
existing_wiki_coverage: research/christophers-rentier-capitalism.md is the wiki's anchor research page for 'rentier capitalism' as a term (itself flagged as based on the publisher description and secondary review coverage rather than a full read of the book). concepts/rentier.md's 'Modern Rentier-Capitalism Literature' section already carries several recent (2026) academic sources sourced from abstract only, each explicitly caveated as such -- Ilan Kapoor (Environment and Planning D, entitlement/exemption framing), Susan J. Smith & Gavin A. Wood (Housing, Theory and Society, owner-occupation edges), and Jose Gabriel Palma (Review of Political Economy, a Ricardian/neoliberal-era reading) -- this is the established precedent and house style for how the wiki handles a source in Bartilow's exact situation (Tier-1-by-rubric author, peer-reviewed venue, abstract-only access). research/lapavitsas-financialization.md is the closest existing research page on the 'financialization' theme, but is qualitative/theoretical (Marxist 'financial expropriation' via debtor wage streams) rather than this paper's quantitative cross-national panel design -- the two are thematically adjacent, not overlapping evidence, and Lapavitsas's page's own 'Bears On' precedent (explicitly distinguishing his wage-extraction channel from the wiki's land-collateral channel) is a useful model for how a Bartilow entry would need to distinguish its top-income-share channel from any land-rent claim. No existing problems/, benefits/, or objections/ page addresses democracy, democratic backsliding, or authoritarianism (checked directly in the repo; only concepts/property-owning-democracy.md and unrelated files under scratchpad/ matched a search for 'democra').
uncertainties: (1) Full article text (introduction, literature review defining 'rentier capitalism' and 'financialization' in the author's own terms, the data/measures section naming the actual financialization index and democracy index used, results tables with coefficients, and discussion) is inaccessible through every access-ladder rung attempted: direct browser-UA curl (403, Cloudflare challenge), r.jina.ai (returns only the same public abstract/metadata the landing page shows a non-subscriber, not the gated body), the synapsesocial.com mirror named in the queue (AI-generated summary only, no full text hosted), and a WebSearch pass for an open preprint or author-hosted copy (none found; Bartilow's own CV, fetched directly, does not yet list this article). Purchasing the USD 56 individual-article PDF was not attempted. A T1 with institutional access to Taylor & Francis / The Social Science Journal should read the full text before drafting any page-length treatment. (2) Whether the paper engages with Christophers's specific sectoral taxonomy of rentier capitalism at all (or only borrows the phrase for its title while using a distinct, narrower income-share operationalization) cannot be confirmed without the literature-review section. (3) The specific financialization and democracy measures, and all effect-size/coefficient magnitudes, are unknown beyond the qualitative 'significantly increases' / 'fully mediated' language in the abstract itself.
